blocks.text: Light and other forms of electromagnetic radiation travel as waves made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields. The waves are described by their wavelength (lambda) and frequency (nu), and they travel at the speed of light, c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. These are related by c = lambda x nu, where lambda is in metres, nu in hertz (s^-1) and c in m/s.

The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays. According to Planck's quantum theory, atoms and molecules emit or absorb only discrete amounts of energy (quanta), and the energy of radiation is directly proportional to its frequency: E = h nu, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 x 10^-34 J s.

blocks.alt: A horizontal band divided into gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave and radio waves, with an arrow showing wavelength increasing to the right, highest energy at the gamma end and lowest at the radio end. The narrow visible part is expanded into a rainbow from 400 to 750 nm. Below: c = lambda x nu and E = h nu = hc/lambda.
blocks.caption: The electromagnetic spectrum and the visible region (original diagram after Figure 29.1).
blocks.long_description: Moving from gamma rays to radio waves the wavelength gets longer, so the frequency and the energy of each photon get smaller. Visible light, 400-750 nm, is only a narrow band; UV-visible spectroscopy uses about 200-800 nm and infrared spectroscopy longer wavelengths.
